topic: Searching and pivoting through logs to reconstruct a sequence of events
title: Triage the overnight auth log
instructions:
## Your first shift in the SOC

You are **abena**, a tier-1 analyst. An alert fired overnight on the student portal server: many failed SSH logins. Work out what happened from **/var/log/auth.log**, write your findings into a **report** directory in your home, and contain the one account that matters.

## Do this

1. Look at the log with `less` or `head`. Notice the shape of a "Failed password" line and an "Accepted" line.
2. Count the failed password lines into `report/failed-count.txt` (`grep -c`).
3. List failed attempts per source address, most first, into `report/failed-by-ip.txt`. Every failure line ends `from ADDRESS port N ssh2`, so the address is field `$(NF-3)` in awk. Then `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.
4. **Pivot**: did any address that failed also log in successfully? Put the matching "Accepted" line(s) into `report/suspicious.txt`.
5. Contain it: lock the account that was logged into from that address with `sudo usermod -L`, pending a password reset with its owner.

hints: `grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > report/failed-by-ip.txt`
Ten failures and then an Accepted line from the same address is the pattern of a guessed password.

checks.label: The failure count is right
checks.message: failed-count.txt should hold the number of "Failed password" lines.

checks.label: Failures per address are counted
checks.message: failed-by-ip.txt should hold uniq -c counts for each source address.

checks.label: The noisiest address is listed first
checks.message: Sort the counts in descending order with sort -rn.

checks.label: The suspicious login is found
checks.message: suspicious.txt should hold the Accepted line from the address that also failed, and nothing else.

checks.label: You counted with uniq -c
checks.message: Use sort | uniq -c to count attempts per address.

realityNote: A SIEM such as Wazuh or Splunk runs these same searches across thousands of hosts, and fail2ban would have blocked 41.66.12.7 after five attempts. The pivot from "many failures" to "then a success" is the step that turns noise into an incident.
